title: Phosphorus and Sulphur
topicTitle: Phosphorus: allotropes; phosphine: preparation, properties and uses; sulphur: allotropes and uses; hydrogen sulphide: preparation, properties and uses; sulphur dioxide: properties and uses; sulphuric acid: properties and uses
notes: **Phosphorus allotropes — overview:** Phosphorus exhibits three major allotropes: white (yellow) P, red P, and black P. White P is the most reactive and toxic, existing as $P_4$ tetrahedra. Red P is polymeric and relatively stable. Black P is the most stable, with a layered structure similar to graphite. All are solids at room temperature but differ dramatically in reactivity.

**White phosphorus — structure and properties:** White P consists of discrete $P_4$ tetrahedron molecules with bond angles of 60° (severe angle strain, making it highly reactive). It is waxy, soft (can be cut with a knife), poisonous, and insoluble in water but soluble in $CS_2$. It glows in the dark (phosphorescence) due to slow oxidation. Stored under water to prevent contact with air.

**White phosphorus — reactions:** Burns in air: $P_4 + 5O_2 \rightarrow P_4O_{10}$ (white smoke of phosphorus pentoxide). Reacts with $Cl_2$: $P_4 + 6Cl_2 \rightarrow 4PCl_3$ (limited $Cl_2$) or $P_4 + 10Cl_2 \rightarrow 4PCl_5$ (excess $Cl_2$). Reacts with NaOH: $P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O \rightarrow PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2$ (hypophosphite — disproportionation reaction).

**Red phosphorus — preparation and properties:** obtained by heating white P at 240°C in an inert atmosphere (sealed tube). It is polymeric — each P atom is bonded to three others in chains and sheets. Red P is non-toxic, odourless, does not glow in the dark, and is insoluble in $CS_2$. It is more stable than white P due to reduced angle strain (bond angles ~108°).

**Red phosphorus — reactions and uses:** When heated strongly, red P vapours condense to white P (reversible conversion). Reacts with $Cl_2$ to form $PCl_3$ and $PCl_5$. Used in safety matches (along with $KClO_3$ and antimony sulphide on the striking surface). Also used in organophosphorus pesticide synthesis and smoke screens (burns to give $P_4O_{10}$ white smoke).

**Black phosphorus — structure and properties:** Prepared by heating red P in a sealed tube at 200°C with a mercury catalyst, or white P at high pressure. It has a layered structure (two forms: $\alpha$ and $\beta$) with each P atom bonded to three others in puckered sheets. It is the most stable allotrope, non-poisonous, insoluble in all solvents, and conducts electricity — unique among P allotropes.

**Phosphine ($PH_3$) — preparation:** Laboratory: $Ca_3P_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3Ca(OH)_2 + 2PH_3\uparrow$ (cold water) or $Ca_3P_2 + 6HCl \rightarrow 3CaCl_2 + 2PH_3\uparrow$. Also by heating P with conc. NaOH: $P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O \rightarrow PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2$. Commercial: hydrolysis of calcium phosphide. Pure $PH_3$ is colourless and odourless.

**Phosphine — properties:** $PH_3$ is a colourless, extremely toxic gas with a rotten fish smell (technical grade has $P_2H_4$ impurity giving garlic odour). It is weakly basic (forms $PH_4I$ with HI). Highly flammable: $PH_3 + 2O_2 \rightarrow H_3PO_4$. Spontaneously flammable when contaminated with $P_2H_4$ (auto-ignites in air). A strong reducing agent: $4AgNO_3 + 2PH_3 \rightarrow 4Ag\downarrow + 2HNO_3 + P_4$.

**Sulphur allotropes — rhombic and monoclinic:** Rhombic sulphur ($\alpha$-$S_8$) consists of crown-shaped $S_8$ rings, stable below 95.5°C, dense (2.07 g/cm³), golden yellow. Monoclinic sulphur ($\beta$-$S_8$) also has $S_8$ rings but packed differently, stable between 95.5°C and 119°C, needle-shaped crystals, density 1.96 g/cm³. Both convert to each other at the transition temperature (95.5°C).

**Sulphur — transition and plastic sulphur:** At 95.5°C (transition temp), rhombic and monoclinic sulphur are in equilibrium. Above 119°C, sulphur melts to a pale yellow liquid ($\lambda$-sulphur). At 160°C, the liquid darkens and becomes viscous as $S_8$ rings open to form long polymeric chains ($\mu$-sulphur). Poured into cold water, it forms 'plastic sulphur' — an amorphous, elastic mass that slowly crystallises back to rhombic.

**Hydrogen sulphide ($H_2S$) — preparation:** In the laboratory, $H_2S$ is prepared in a Kipp's apparatus: $FeS + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2S\uparrow$ or $FeS + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + H_2S\uparrow$. Cannot use $HNO_3$ (oxidises $H_2S$) or conc. $H_2SO_4$ (oxidises $H_2S$ to S). $H_2S$ is a colourless gas with a characteristic rotten egg smell, highly toxic (LD50 ~300 ppm).

**Hydrogen sulphide — properties and reactions:** Weak diprotic acid in water: $H_2S \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HS^-$, $HS^- \rightleftharpoons H^+ + S^{2-}$ ($K_{a1} = 10^{-7}$, $K_{a2} = 10^{-14}$). Precipitates metal sulphides: $CuSO_4 + H_2S \rightarrow CuS\downarrow (black) + H_2SO_4$; $Pb(CH_3COO)_2 + H_2S \rightarrow PbS\downarrow (black) + 2CH_3COOH$. Burns in air: $2H_2S + 3O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + 2SO_2$.

**Sulphur dioxide ($SO_2$) — preparation and properties:** Prepared by burning sulphur: $S + O_2 \rightarrow SO_2$, or by heating copper with conc. $H_2SO_4$: $Cu + 2H_2SO_4 \rightarrow CuSO_4 + SO_2 + 2H_2O$. It is a colourless gas with a pungent, choking odour. Acidic: $SO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow H_2SO_3$ (sulphurous acid). A reducing agent: turns acidified $K_2Cr_2O_7$ from orange to green ($Cr^{3+}$).

**Sulphur dioxide — bleaching and oxidising action:** $SO_2$ bleaches by reduction (unlike $Cl_2$ which bleaches by oxidation): $SO_2 + H_2O + [O] \rightarrow H_2SO_4$ — the nascent hydrogen reduces the dye. Bleaching is temporary (reversed on standing in air). $SO_2$ also acts as an oxidising agent with $H_2S$: $SO_2 + 2H_2S \rightarrow 2H_2O + 3S\downarrow$ (yellow precipitate).

**Contact process — $H_2SO_4$ manufacture:** Step 1: Burn sulphur/FeS₂ to get $SO_2$. Step 2: Purify gases (remove dust, arsenic). Step 3: Oxidise $SO_2$ to $SO_3$ over $V_2O_5$ catalyst at 450°C, 1-2 atm: $2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3$, $\Delta H = -196\,\text{kJ}$. Step 4: Absorb $SO_3$ in conc. $H_2SO_4$ to form oleum ($H_2S_2O_7$): $SO_3 + H_2S_2O_7 \rightarrow 2H_2SO_4$. Step 5: Dilute oleum with water to get desired concentration.

**Sulphuric acid — the 'king of chemicals':** Conc. $H_2SO_4$ is a strong dehydrating agent (chars sugar: $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} 12C + 11H_2O$ — black foam). It is a strong oxidising agent when hot: $Cu + 2H_2SO_4 \xrightarrow{\Delta} CuSO_4 + SO_2 + 2H_2O$. It is non-volatile, used to prepare volatile acids: $NaCl + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow NaHSO_4 + HCl$ (below 200°C). Used in batteries, fertilizers, dyes, and petroleum refining.
confusion: ❌ Confusing white P and red P — thinking red P is more reactive. ✅ White P is the MOST reactive allotrope due to 60° bond angles (angle strain in $P_4$). Red P is polymeric with relaxed bond angles (~108°) and is far more stable. White P must be stored under water; red P can be handled in air.

❌ Thinking $PH_3$ is acidic like $H_2S$. ✅ $PH_3$ is weakly BASIC (can accept a proton to form $PH_4^+$), while $H_2S$ is weakly acidic. This reversal down the group occurs because P is less electronegative than S, making the P–H bond less polar and the lone pair on P more available for protonation.

❌ Using $HNO_3$ to prepare $H_2S$ from FeS. ✅ $HNO_3$ is an oxidising agent and would oxidise $H_2S$ to sulphur: $H_2S + 2HNO_3 \rightarrow 2NO_2 + S + 2H_2O$. Only non-oxidising acids (dil. HCl or dil. $H_2SO_4$) should be used in a Kipp's apparatus.

❌ Confusing $SO_2$ bleaching (reduction) with $Cl_2$ bleaching (oxidation). ✅ $SO_2$ bleaches by reduction — the coloured dye is reduced to a colourless form. This is temporary (air re-oxidises it). $Cl_2$ bleaches by oxidation (nascent oxygen) — this is permanent. The mechanisms are opposite.

❌ Thinking rhombic and monoclinic sulphur have different molecular formulas. ✅ Both consist of $S_8$ crown-shaped rings. The difference is in crystal packing: rhombic has a orthorhombic lattice, monoclinic has a monoclinic lattice. They are polymorphs, not different molecules.

❌ Believing conc. $H_2SO_4$ is used to prepare HI from KI. ✅ Conc. $H_2SO_4$ oxidises $HI$ to $I_2$: $2HI + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow I_2 + SO_2 + 2H_2O$. Non-oxidising acids like $H_3PO_4$ must be used: $KI + H_3PO_4 \rightarrow KH_2PO_4 + HI$. This is a classic exception to the 'non-volatile acid displaces volatile acid' rule.

❌ Thinking $SO_2$ is only a reducing agent. ✅ $SO_2$ is primarily a reducing agent (oxidises to $SO_4^{2-}$), but it can also act as an oxidising agent: with $H_2S$, $SO_2 + 2H_2S \rightarrow 2H_2O + 3S\downarrow$ (here S in $SO_2$ goes from +4 to 0). This dual behaviour is common for elements in intermediate oxidation states.
practice: Calculate the mass of $P_4O_{10}$ formed when 6.2 g of white phosphorus burns completely in oxygen. (P = 31, O = 16). Solution: $P_4 + 5O_2 \rightarrow P_4O_{10}$. Moles of $P_4$ = 6.2/124 = 0.05 mol. Moles of $P_4O_{10}$ = 0.05 mol. Molar mass = 284 g. Mass = 0.05 × 284 = 14.2 g.

How many litres of $PH_3$ (at STP) are produced when 1 mol of $Ca_3P_2$ reacts with excess water? Solution: $Ca_3P_2 + 6H_2O \rightarrow 3Ca(OH)_2 + 2PH_3$. 1 mol $Ca_3P_2$ gives 2 mol $PH_3$. Volume = 2 × 22.4 = 44.8 L at STP.

In the preparation of $H_2S$, 11.6 g of FeS reacts with excess HCl. Calculate the volume of $H_2S$ at STP. (Fe = 56, S = 32). Solution: $FeS + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2S$. Molar mass of FeS = 88 g. Moles = 11.6/88 = 0.1318 mol. Volume of $H_2S$ = 0.1318 × 22.4 = 2.95 L at STP.

Calculate the mass of sulphur precipitated when 6.72 L of $SO_2$ (at STP) reacts completely with $H_2S$. Solution: $SO_2 + 2H_2S \rightarrow 2H_2O + 3S\downarrow$. Moles of $SO_2$ = 6.72/22.4 = 0.3 mol. Moles of S = 3 × 0.3 = 0.9 mol. Mass of S = 0.9 × 32 = 28.8 g.

In the contact process, 128 g of $SO_2$ is converted to $H_2SO_4$ with 90% yield. Calculate the mass of $H_2SO_4$ produced. (S = 32, O = 16, H = 1). Solution: Moles of $SO_2$ = 128/64 = 2 mol. Theoretical $H_2SO_4$ = 2 mol (1:1 ratio). Molar mass = 98 g. Theoretical mass = 196 g. Actual = 90% × 196 = 176.4 g.

How many grams of conc. $H_2SO_4$ (98%) are needed to dehydrate 34.2 g of sucrose ($C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}$)? Solution: $C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} 12C + 11H_2O$. Moles of sucrose = 34.2/342 = 0.1 mol. Moles of $H_2O$ produced = 1.1 mol. $H_2SO_4$ acts as dehydrating agent (not consumed stoichiometrically, but we need enough to absorb 1.1 mol H₂O). Mass of water = 19.8 g. Minimum conc. $H_2SO_4$ needed ≈ 20.2 g of 98% acid (assuming it absorbs all water).
universalFacts: White phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by Hennig Brand while searching for the philosopher's stone — he made it by boiling urine and condensing the vapours. The name 'phosphorus' means 'light-bearer' in Greek, referring to its glow in the dark.

The contact process for sulphuric acid produces over 200 million tonnes annually worldwide, making it one of the most produced chemicals on Earth. Sulphuric acid consumption is often used as an index of a nation's industrial development.

Hydrogen sulphide is not just a toxic gas — it is produced naturally in sewers, swamps, and volcanic gases, and is also a signalling molecule in mammalian biology at low concentrations, regulating blood vessel dilation and inflammation.

Black phosphorus, the most stable allotrope, was first synthesised in 1914 but only recently (2014) gained attention as a 2D semiconductor with a tunable band gap (~0.3-2.0 eV), making it a promising candidate for next-generation electronics beyond silicon.

The $S_8$ crown structure of rhombic sulphur was confirmed by X-ray crystallography in 1925. Each sulphur atom is bonded to two neighbours at 108° angles with S–S bond length of 2.06 Å — remarkably similar to the bond angles in cyclohexane's chair conformation.
